findings.title: Compaction count write is split across two kernels with fragile ordering dependency
findings.description: The compact() method launches k_last_offset_count (dim=1, always writes _count2) and k_compact_alive_scatter (dim=capacity, conditionally writes _count2 only when the last particle is alive). If k_last_offset_count were removed or the launch order reversed, k_compact_alive_scatter would fail to write the final count when the last particle is dead (alive[tid]==0 triggers early return on line 50 before line 60's count write). This creates a fragile implicit dependency between the two kernels where correct behavior relies on sequential ordering and both kernels being present.
findings.impact: If this code is refactored (e.g., k_last_offset_count removed as 'redundant', or launch order swapped), compaction silently produces a stale count when the last particle is dead. This corrupts the particle count for all subsequent operations, leading to reading stale particle data, incorrect indexing, and simulation instability or crashes.
findings.fix: Consolidate count computation into one kernel. Either (a) have k_compact_alive_scatter always write count_out unconditionally after the scatter loop using a separate warp-level reduction, or (b) keep k_last_offset_count as the sole count writer and remove the conditional count_out write from k_compact_alive_scatter entirely.

findings.title: Whitewater compact scatter passes write-target arrays via inputs instead of outputs
findings.description: k_ww_compact_scatter writes to _position2, _velocity2, _age2, _life2, and _count2, but all except _count2 are passed via the inputs parameter rather than outputs. In the current non-differentiable mode (wp.set_module_options({'enable_backward': False})), Warp permits writes to input arrays, so this works. However, if autograd were ever enabled, input arrays would be treated as constants and writes would not be propagated. The k_ww_compact_scatter kernel body on lines 435-438 also never writes to out_count despite it being declared and listed in outputs. This mismatch between declared intent and actual I/O creates a latent hazard.
findings.impact: Enabling autograd (removing the backward=False flag) would silently break whitewater compaction — write targets in inputs would not receive kernel outputs, causing whitewater particle data loss and count corruption. The unused out_count parameter also creates confusion about which kernel is responsible for the final count.
findings.fix: Move all write-target arrays (_position2, _velocity2, _age2, _life2) from inputs to outputs in the k_ww_compact_scatter launch call. Remove the out_count parameter from k_ww_compact_scatter entirely since the kernel never writes it, and rely solely on k_ww_final_count for the count. Remove the unnecessary self._count2.zero_() on line 395.

findings.title: Particle compaction scatter passes write-target arrays via inputs creating latent autograd hazard
findings.description: The k_compact_alive_scatter kernel writes to _position2, _velocity2, _attrs2 arrays, and _count2, but all are passed via the inputs parameter of wp.launch rather than outputs. In the current non-differentiable module configuration, Warp allows writes to inputs, so the code works. However, this is semantically incorrect and would break if autograd were enabled or if Warp's behavior changes. The same issue appears in the particles.py compact() method where all double-buffer targets are listed as inputs despite being write destinations.
findings.impact: Enabling autograd or upgrading to a Warp version that enforces input immutability would cause compaction to silently discard particle data, corrupting all downstream simulations. Particle positions, velocities, and attributes would not be properly compacted.
findings.fix: Move all write-target arrays (_position2, _velocity2, and all _attrs2 entries) from the inputs list to the outputs list in the wp.launch call for k_compact_alive_scatter at line 134. Also move _count2 to outputs for semantic clarity, even though it is also written by k_last_offset_count.

findings.title: Whitewater compaction uses sliced arrays for scan but full arrays for kernel causing subtle aliasing dependency
findings.description: The compact() method computes the scan on sliced views (self.alive[:n], self._scan[:n]) when n < capacity (line 377-381), but passes full arrays (self.alive, self._scan) to k_ww_compact_scatter and k_ww_final_count. This is functionally correct because kernel tid is bounded by dim=n, so only the first n elements are accessed. However, this creates a fragile aliasing assumption: the scan output in self._scan[n:] is NOT guaranteed to be valid, and any kernel that accidentally accesses beyond index n-1 would read stale data. Additionally, k_ww_final_count at line 443-448 receives n as a scalar int but computes scan[n-1] without verifying n > 0, relying on the early return at line 375-376 which only checks n==0.
findings.impact: If the early-return guard at line 375 were removed or modified, k_ww_final_count would access scan[-1] causing undefined behavior (GPU out-of-bounds access or hang). The sliced-vs-full asymmetry is also a maintenance hazard.
findings.fix: Add an explicit guard in k_ww_final_count: if n <= 0: out_count[0] = 0; return. Alternatively, keep the sliced approach throughout by passing self.alive[:n] and self._scan[:n] to all kernels for clarity.

findings.title: Particle compaction always scans full capacity array regardless of active particle count
findings.description: compact() calls wp.utils.array_scan(self.alive, self.scan_tmp, inclusive=False) on the entire capacity-sized array (line 124), then launches k_compact_alive_scatter with dim=self.capacity (line 132). When the active particle count is small relative to capacity (e.g., 1,000 particles in a 2,000,000-capacity system), this wastes GPU compute on 1,999,000 threads that immediately exit at the 'if tid >= n: return' check. This is a performance issue scaling with O(capacity) rather than O(active_count).
findings.impact: Unnecessary GPU thread launch overhead and scan computation proportional to maximum capacity rather than active particle count. For large capacities (millions) with few active particles, this can significantly inflate per-substep GPU time, reducing interactive viewport frame rates.
findings.fix: Slice arrays to active count similar to the whitewater compact: n = int(self.count.numpy()[0]); if n == 0: return; then scan self.alive[:n] into self.scan_tmp[:n] and launch scatter with dim=n. Add a k_reset_alive pass for the unused tail (beyond n) or add an explicit zero to the else branch.

findings.title: P2G velocity splat accumulates into grid fields that may contain stale sourcing velocity without weight reset
findings.description: In _p2g(), k_particle_set_grid_data atomically adds particle velocity contributions to grid faces using the existing velocity and weight fields. These fields were modified by _source() earlier in the substep (field-mode sourcing writes velocity directly without setting corresponding weights). The k_normalize_mac kernel at line 777 only divides by weight where weight > 1e-8. Voxels with field-sourced velocity but zero P2G weight retain the raw sourced velocity without normalization. Voxels with both sourced velocity AND particle contributions get an admixture: weight comes only from particles, so the normalization produces (sourced_vel + particle_weighted_vel) / particle_weight_total, which is a blended value where the sourced contribution's weight is implicitly 1.0 regardless of how many particles contributed.
findings.impact: Velocity in voxels that are both field-sourced and particle-filled is numerically inconsistent — the field-source velocity effectively gets unit weight in the normalization while particle contributions are weighted by trilinear scatter weights. This creates subtle velocity biases at source-region boundaries that can affect FLIP/PIC advection accuracy. In practice the impact varies by scene but may produce visible artifacts where source shapes overlap particle-filled regions.
findings.fix: Either (a) track field-source weight contributions separately and add them to the weight arrays during sourcing, or (b) clear source-injected velocity from grid cells that receive P2G weight above a threshold (i.e., let particles fully overwrite sourced velocity). Option (a) is more physically correct but requires additional kernel changes.

findings.title: Particle emission on capacity overflow uses return instead of break, skipping subsequent shapes for that voxel
findings.description: In k_source_shapes_particles, when the particle buffer fills up (slot >= capacity), the thread executes 'return' at line 331 (via the early-exit path after atomic_sub). This 'return' exits the entire kernel invocation for that thread, not just the current shape's emission loop. Any remaining shapes (shapes at higher indices in the same voxel) are silently skipped. While capacity overflow is an error condition, the silent shape-skipping behavior is not communicated to the user.
findings.impact: When particle capacity is exhausted, voxels with multiple overlapping source shapes may only receive particles from the first shape(s), creating an uneven particle distribution. The remaining shapes' particles are lost without warning, which could cause unexpected visual artifacts in scenes with multiple emitters.
findings.fix: Replace 'return' with 'break' to exit only the current shape's emission loop rather than terminating the entire thread. After the capacity guard, the thread should continue to process remaining shapes (which will also find capacity exhausted and break). This is more consistent and predictable.

findings.title: Whitewater advection writes to alive flag and position/velocity without memory ordering guarantees
findings.description: In k_advect_whitewater, the kernel reads ww_alive[tid] at line 236, then writes ww_age[tid] at line 286, ww_alive[tid] at lines 288 and 293, and finally ww_positions[tid] and ww_velocities[tid] at lines 295-296. While thread-independent access (each tid is unique) means no race condition between threads, the write to ww_alive[tid]=0 (kill) happens before position/velocity are written. If another kernel were to read ww_velocities[tid] while this kernel is writing (not possible in sequential Warp launches), it could see inconsistent state. No actual bug exists in the current sequential launch flow.
findings.impact: None in current implementation. Noted as a future-concurrency hazard if async launch patterns are adopted.
findings.fix: No immediate action required. If async/stream execution is added in the future, ensure writes to particle state are ordered after the kill decision via explicit synchronization or per-particle barriers.

findings.title: Particle count update after compaction uses device copy instead of pointer swap
findings.description: In compact(), after swapping all particle attribute buffers (position, velocity, attrs), the count is updated via 'wp.copy(self.count, self._count2)' (line 151) rather than a pointer swap like the attribute buffers. This copies the device scalar from the temporary count buffer to the active count buffer. Meanwhile, WhitewaterSystem.compact() uses a swap (line 407: self.count, self._count2 = self._count2, self.count). The inconsistency is cosmetic — both approaches produce the same result — but the copy approach leaves _count2 with the old value, while the swap approach makes _count2 the previous count. This means after compact(), ParticleSystem._count2 holds junk (pre-compact count) while WhitewaterSystem._count2 holds the post-compact count from the swap.
findings.impact: If any code path reads _count2 between compacts (none currently do), the particle system would read the pre-compact stale value while the whitewater system would read the current count. This asymmetry is a maintenance trap.
findings.fix: Adopt the same pattern in both systems. Either use wp.copy in both (explicit, predictable) or pointer swap in both (zero-copy, leaves _count2 as old count). The swap approach is preferred for consistency with the attribute buffer handling.

findings.title: Trilinear sample uses unnormalized weights when all 8 neighbors are unallocated
findings.description: sample_scalar_trilinear iterates over 8 neighbor voxels. When all 8 are unallocated (flat < 0 for all), wsum remains 0.0, and the function returns the default value at line 186 (return default). This is correct behavior. However, if even one neighbor is allocated, the weights are summed only over allocated neighbors (the else branch at line 182 adds to both acc and wsum, but allocated-only). If some neighbors are allocated and others are not, the weight sum excludes unallocated contributions, and the normalization on line 185 divides by the partial sum. This renormalization is standard for boundary handling but means the fallback weight distribution is non-uniform near domain edges.
findings.impact: Minimal. Sampled values near unallocated domain boundaries will have slightly different interpolation characteristics than interior samples. This affects surface SDF sampling and velocity interpolation near grid boundaries.
findings.fix: Document this behavior explicitly in the docstring. If uniform trilinear weights are required near boundaries, pad the sparse grid with allocated ghost leaves at domain borders.
